title: Given an array containing `n` distinct numbers taken from the range `1` to `n` (or `0` to `n-1`), sort the array in place in O(n) time and O(1) extra space without using any sorting library. Explain the Cyclic Sort pattern and where it applies.
shortTitle: Cyclic Sort (Place Each Number at Its Correct Index)
keyPoints: When values are a permutation of 1 to n, each value tells you its correct index: value v belongs at index v - 1
Swap the current value to its home index repeatedly until the current slot holds the correct value, then advance
Each swap places at least one number in its final position, so at most n swaps occur across the entire run
The algorithm is O(n) time and O(1) space, beating O(n log n) comparison sorts for this special case
Guard with value comparison (nums[i] != nums[j]) instead of index comparison for safety with duplicates
The pattern powers missing-number and duplicate-detection variants where a mismatch after sorting reveals the answer
Only applies when the value range is known and dense; it is not a general-purpose sort

s1_definition.oneliner: When values are a permutation of 1 to n, the value itself tells you its home index, so one swap-until-correct pass sorts in linear time.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Cyclic Sort** – an in-place sorting technique for arrays whose values form a known contiguous range (typically 1 to n or 0 to n - 1).
- **Home index rule** – value v belongs at index v - 1 (for 1 to n range), so each value has exactly one correct position.
- **Swap-until-correct** – keep swapping the current element to its home index until the current slot holds the right value, then advance the pointer.
- **Amortized O(n)** – each swap settles at least one number permanently, and there are only n numbers, so at most n swaps total.
- **Pattern family** – the same place-at-index idea solves missing number, find all duplicates, and find the first missing positive.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India numbers its safe deposit lockers 1 to n, and at closing the keys are scattered on the counter. Key 5 belongs in locker 5, key 1 in locker 1. Rajesh picks up whatever key is in front of him, walks it to its matching locker, and takes whatever key was already there. He keeps swapping until the front slot holds the right key, then moves to the next slot. No key is carried twice unnecessarily, so the whole counter is tidied in one disciplined pass.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Cyclic Sort: Place Each Value at Its Home Index

  Home rule: value v → index v-1

  Input: [3, 1, 5, 4, 2]

  i=0: nums[0]=3, home=2, nums[0]!=nums[2] → swap(0,2)
       [5, 1, 3, 4, 2]  (3 is now at index 2 ✓)
  i=0: nums[0]=5, home=4, nums[0]!=nums[4] → swap(0,4)
       [2, 1, 3, 4, 5]  (5 is now at index 4 ✓)
  i=0: nums[0]=2, home=1, nums[0]!=nums[1] → swap(0,1)
       [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]  (2 at index 1 ✓, 1 at index 0 ✓)
  i=0: nums[0]=1, home=0, nums[0]==nums[0] → advance i=1
  i=1: nums[1]=2, home=1 → advance i=2
  i=2: nums[2]=3, home=2 → advance i=3
  i=3: nums[3]=4, home=3 → advance i=4
  i=4: nums[4]=5, home=4 → advance i=5 → DONE

  Result: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]  (3 swaps for n=5)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Cyclic Sort is an in-place linear-time technique that applies when the array values form a known dense range such as 1 to n. The defining insight is that each value has exactly one correct home index, namely value minus one, so instead of comparing elements against each other you simply carry each value to its rightful slot.

You keep a pointer at the current position, compute the target index from the value there, and swap it home if it is not already correct. Critically, you do not advance the pointer after a swap because the element that just arrived may itself be misplaced. The reason it runs in linear time is amortized: every swap permanently settles at least one number, and there are only n numbers, so at most n swaps ever occur.

Guard the swap with a value comparison rather than an index comparison, which keeps the loop safe even if duplicates appear. That same place-at-index habit is what powers the missing-number and duplicate-detection variants: after sorting, any position where `nums[i] != i + 1` reveals the anomaly.

At the National Bank of India, Rajesh used this in the nightly settlement batch where sequence numbers arrived as a permutation of 1 to n. Cyclic Sort arranged them in a single disciplined pass with no extra memory, and the same pattern detected any missing sequence numbers immediately after sorting.

Remember one sentence: when values map to indices, swap each to its home and the whole array is sorted in at most n swaps.
